analysis.one_liner: Cancels up to $50,000 in student loan debt per borrower and lets private loans be converted to federal loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2019 with 11 cosponsors, sent to three committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Department of Education automatically cancel up to $50,000 of student loan debt per borrower, with full cancellation for people making under $100,000 and partial cancellation for those above it. It would pause payments, interest, and collections for a year while the cancellation was carried out, refinance remaining federal loans at lower rates from the 2016-2017 school year, let private student loan borrowers convert their loans into federal ones, and make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy. It also cancels debt in private loan conversions and excludes Members of Congress from receiving any cancellation.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 43 million Americans holding federal student loans would get automatic cancellation of up to $50,000, and private loan borrowers could convert to federal loans and qualify too. Borrowers in default would get the default removed from their credit records and wage garnishments would stop for a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, especially those under $100,000 income

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Education must automatically discharge up to $50,000 of federal student loan debt per borrower within 12 months, without requiring any application or regard to default status [S2][S3].
Borrowers with adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less get the maximum cancellation; higher earners lose $1 of cancellation for every $3 of income above that threshold [S2][S3].
For one year, all federal loan borrowers are automatically placed in forbearance: no payments due, no interest accrues, and the government may not garnish wages or pursue collections [S2][S3].
Borrowers with private student loans can convert them to federal loans at 2016-2017 interest rates, making them eligible for cancellation; canceled debt is excluded from taxable income [S2][S3].
Student loans would become dischargeable in bankruptcy like other consumer debt, by striking the special exception in the bankruptcy code [S2][S3].
Borrowers whose loans were in default would have the default removed from their credit history once the loan is discharged [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost of canceling the debt and of refinancing older loans at lower rates, since the Department of Education would collect less on loans it holds or guarantees. Private student lenders would lose loans converted to federal loans and discharged, and loan servicers and collectors would lose the accounts and collection work that disappear with the debt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, private lenders, and loan servicers

drawbacks.text: The cost is substantial: canceling up to $50,000 per federal borrower and refinancing remaining balances at 2016-2017 rates would eliminate or reduce a large federal asset, with the cost borne by taxpayers through the federal budget [S2][S3].

The cancellation is based on income from the most recent tax year, so some people with high past incomes but lower current incomes would get reduced cancellation, and some borrowers whose loans are held by institutions must go through holder-based discharge mechanisms rather than automatic erasure [S3].

The bill requires the Education Department to implement an enormous automatic discharge, refinancing, and private-loan conversion program on tight deadlines (discharge within 12 months, private-loan conversion window of only a few months), an administrative lift with real execution risk [S3].

Because up to $50,000 is forgiven per person regardless of remaining debt level, some relief flows to borrowers with relatively small balances or strong finances, though the income phase-down limits this above $100,000 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to borrowers is large and immediate: millions of households would see debt of up to $50,000 erased, payments and collections paused, and credit records repaired, with canceled debt shielded from taxes. The tradeoff is a substantial cost to the federal budget and to private lenders, and the benefits tilt toward borrowers under $100,000 in income while higher earners get partial relief. The main honest criticisms are the price to taxpayers and the demanding implementation timeline, not the design of the relief itself.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House committees it was referred to — never even getting a subcommittee vote in Judiciary — and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Clyburn introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, with Reps. Schakowsky, Khanna, and Clarke of New York as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Eleven House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total [S4].

The bill was referred to three committees — Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — on the day it was introduced, meaning each would have to act on the parts in its jurisdiction [S1][S5].

The only further action in the entire two-year Congress was a referral to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law on August 12, 2019; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill never received a vote in either chamber and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers, private lenders, and debt collectors keep their accounts and collection revenue, and taxpayers avoid the cost of the cancellation — while borrowers continue to owe their loans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Loan servicers, private lenders, and debt collectors

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Canceled debt means canceled servicing contracts and collection work, including an end to wage garnishment during the pause period. Servicers lose revenue but borrowers gain relief.

Borrowers could convert private loans into federal loans that would then be canceled, paying off and erasing the lenders' loans at low 2016-2017 rates. Lenders would also face new reporting requirements on their loan portfolios.

The Treasury and Education Department would give up the value of canceled and refinanced loans, a multi-hundred-billion-dollar budget cost, in exchange for relieving millions of borrowers of debt. The bill also requires data-sharing between Treasury and Education to determine each borrower's income-based cancellation amount.
